# Assignment 1: Importing Data into R

This assignment demonstrates how to import data from several common sources in R, including Excel files, statistical package formats, text/XML/web sources, and databases.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r install-packages}
required_packages <- c("readxl", "writexl", "foreign", "haven", "rvest", "xml2", "jsonlite", "DBI", "RSQLite")
for (pkg in required_packages) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}

library(readxl)
library(writexl)
library(foreign)
library(haven)
library(rvest)
library(xml2)
library(jsonlite)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
```

```{r create-folder}
dir.create("datasets", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Package guide

The following R packages were installed to support the data import examples in this assignment:

- `readxl`: reads Excel files (`.xlsx`, `.xls`)
- `writexl`: writes data to Excel files
- `foreign`: reads older statistical files such as SAS and SPSS data files
- `haven`: reads and writes SAS, SPSS, and Stata files
- `rvest`: scrapes HTML content from web pages
- `xml2`: reads and writes XML files
- `jsonlite`: reads and writes JSON files
- `DBI`: provides a common interface for database connections
- `RSQLite`: connects R to SQLite databases

## Data generation: create all datasets first

```{r seed-all-datasets}
students <- data.frame(
  student_id = 1:4,
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "Diana"),
  age = c(20, 22, 21, 23),
  score = c(88, 91, 85, 94)
)

write_xlsx(students, path = "datasets/students.xlsx")
write_xpt(students, path = "datasets/students_sas.xpt")
write_sav(students, path = "datasets/students_spss.sav")
write.dta(students, file = "datasets/students_stata.dta")

write.table(
  students,
  file = "datasets/students.txt",
  sep = ",",
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = TRUE
)

json_data <- jsonlite::toJSON(split(students, seq_len(nrow(students))), pretty = TRUE)
writeLines(json_data, "datasets/students.json")

xml_content <- '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<students>
  <student>
    <student_id>1</student_id>
    <name>Alice</name>
    <age>20</age>
    <score>88</score>
  </student>
  <student>
    <student_id>2</student_id>
    <name>Bob</name>
    <age>22</age>
    <score>91</score>
  </student>
  <student>
    <student_id>3</student_id>
    <name>Charlie</name>
    <age>21</age>
    <score>85</score>
  </student>
</students>'

write_xml(read_xml(charToRaw(xml_content)), "datasets/students.xml")

con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "datasets/students.db")
dbWriteTable(con, "students", students, overwrite = TRUE)
dbDisconnect(con)
```

## 1. Loading data from Excel

Excel files are commonly used in business and research settings. The `readxl` package can read `.xls` and `.xlsx` files.

```{r excel-import}
# Read the Excel file into R for analysis.
excel_data <- read_excel("datasets/students.xlsx")
print(excel_data)
```

## 2. Loading data from statistical packages (SAS, SPSS, Stata)

Different statistical software stores datasets in different formats. Below are examples for SAS transport files, SPSS `.sav` files, and Stata `.dta` files.

### SAS transport file

```{r sas-import}
# Import a SAS transport file using the haven package.
sas_data <- read_xpt("datasets/students_sas.xpt")
print(sas_data)
```

### SPSS file

```{r spss-import}
# Import an SPSS dataset saved in .sav format.
spss_data <- read_sav("datasets/students_spss.sav")
print(spss_data)
```

### Stata file

```{r stata-import}
# Import a Stata dataset stored in .dta format.
stata_data <- read.dta("datasets/students_stata.dta")
print(stata_data)
```

## 3. Loading data from text files, JSON, XML, and web scraping

### Text file (ASCII/CSV)

```{r text-file-import}
# CSV files can be read directly with read.csv().
text_data_csv <- read.csv("datasets/students.txt")
print(text_data_csv[, c("student_id", "age", "score")])

# read.table() is a more general option when the separator must be specified.
text_data_table <- read.table("datasets/students.txt", header = TRUE, sep = ",")
print(text_data_table[, c("student_id", "age", "score")])
```

### JSON file

```{r json-import}
# Read the JSON file and convert it into a data frame.
json_data <- jsonlite::fromJSON("datasets/students.json")
student_df_json <- do.call(rbind, lapply(json_data, function(x) as.data.frame(x, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
print(student_df_json)
```

### XML file

```{r xml-import}
# Read the XML file and convert the student nodes into a data frame.
parsed_xml <- read_xml("datasets/students.xml")
student_nodes <- xml_find_all(parsed_xml, "//student")
student_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(student_nodes, function(node) {
  data.frame(
    student_id = as.integer(xml_text(xml_find_first(node, "student_id"))),
    name = xml_text(xml_find_first(node, "name")),
    age = as.integer(xml_text(xml_find_first(node, "age"))),
    score = as.integer(xml_text(xml_find_first(node, "score"))),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
print(student_df)
```

### Web scraping

```{r web-scraping}
# Web scraping reads page content from a URL and extracts the title.
web_page <- read_html("https://example.com")
page_title <- html_text(html_nodes(web_page, "title"))
print(page_title)
```

## 4. Loading data from a database management system

A database is often used to store large amounts of structured data. In this example, we create a SQLite database and query it using R.

```{r database-import}
# Connect to the SQLite database and query the table.
con <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "datasets/students.db")
result <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM students")
print(result)
dbDisconnect(con)
```

## Conclusion

R provides a wide range of tools to import datasets from different source formats. Common examples include:

- Excel files with `readxl`
- Statistical software files with `foreign` and `haven`
- Text files with `read.csv()` and `read.table()`
- XML and HTML/web sources with `xml2` and `rvest`
- Databases with `DBI` and `RSQLite`

These methods allow analysts to bring data into R efficiently for cleaning, transformation, and analysis.
